    AI Overview
    Extensively drug-resistant (XDR) Shigella infections are rising in the U.S., with 8.5% of samples in 2023 resistant to standard antibiotics, including azithromycin and ciprofloxacin. These bacteria cause severe, contagious diarrhea (shigellosis) and are particularly risky for children and immunocompromised adults. No FDA-approved oral treatment currently exists for these strains. 
    Key Details on Drug-Resistant Shigella 
    • Definition: XDR Shigella is resistant to all standard antibiotic treatments: ampicillin, azithromycin, ceftriaxone, ciprofloxacin, and trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole (TMP-SMX).
    • Rising Threat: Cases have grown substantially since 2016, with 12% of California cases being XDR as of May 2024, representing a 78% increase from 2023.
    • Symptoms: Intense diarrhea (often bloody), fever, and stomach pain.
    • High-Risk Groups: While anyone can be infected, cases are high among adult men, particularly gay or bisexual men, international travelers, and people with compromised immune systems.
    • Transmission: Spread easily through fecal-oral contact (contaminated food, water, or surfaces). 
    Treatment and Prevention 
    • Limited Options: Because standard antibiotics often fail, doctors may need to manage symptoms with fluids, as most infections resolve on their own in about a week.
    • Prevention: Thorough handwashing with soap and water is crucial.
    • Precautions: Avoid swimming in pools, lakes, or ponds when infected or for several days after diarrhea stops. 
    For more information, visit the CDC's page on antimicrobial-resistant Shigella.

    What antibiotic is drug-resistant Shigella resistant to?
    Multidrug-resistant (MDR) Shigella:

    For this report, we have defined MDR Shigella as resistant to three or more of the five established antibiotics used to treat Shigella infections: azithromycin, fluroquinolones (e.g. ciprofloxacin), third- generation cephalosporins (e.g. ceftriaxone), TMP-SMX, and ampicillin.
